_metadata.description: Disease-specific management guidance for PlantVillage classes.
_metadata.disclaimer: This information is for general guidance only. Always consult a qualified agricultural extension officer or plant pathologist before applying any treatment. Do not rely solely on this system for crop management decisions.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Disease Fact Sheets

Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is one of the most common apple diseases worldwide. It produces olive-green to brown lesions on leaves and fruit surfaces, often causing early leaf drop and misshapen or cracked fruit.
symptoms: Olive-green or brown spots on leaves
Velvety fungal growth on lesions
Scabby, cracked spots on fruit
Premature leaf and fruit drop in severe infections
management: Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves in autumn to break the disease cycle.
Apply approved fungicides (e.g., captan or myclobutanil) during early spring when infection periods are forecast.
Prune trees to improve canopy airflow and reduce humidity.
Plant scab-resistant apple varieties where feasible.
preventive_measures: Monitor weather forecasts; apply preventive sprays before rainy periods.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
Maintain good orchard sanitation throughout the season.
consult_expert_if: Severe defoliation occurs early in the season.
Fungicide-resistant strains are suspected (poor control despite timely sprays).
More than 20% of fruit are affected.

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot affects apples, causing circular brown lesions on fruit (often with concentric rings), leaf spots, and cankers on branches. Infected fruit eventually mummify and remain on the tree.
symptoms: Circular, brown to black lesions on fruit with alternating light and dark rings
Purple-bordered leaf spots turning brown at centre
Cankers with sunken, cracked bark on branches
management: Prune out and destroy all cankers and dead wood.
Remove mummified fruit from the tree and ground.
Apply fungicides (e.g., captan, thiophanate-methyl) during the growing season according to label directions.
Reduce tree stress through proper fertilisation and irrigation.
preventive_measures: Maintain orchard sanitation – remove dead wood promptly.
Avoid wounding trees during pruning when wet.
Ensure good airflow through canopy.
consult_expert_if: Large cankers appear on main scaffolding branches.
Disease spreads rapidly despite management.
Resistant cultivar options are needed.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease requiring two hosts – eastern red cedar (juniper) for winter spore production and apple for spring infection. It causes bright orange-yellow lesions on apple leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surface in spring
Orange, tube-like structures (aecia) on undersides of lesions
Deformed fruit with orange-red discolouration
management: Remove nearby eastern red cedar or juniper hosts where practical.
Apply protectant fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil, mancozeb) at pink bud and petal fall stages.
Plant rust-resistant apple varieties.
preventive_measures: Survey surrounding area for cedar galls in late winter; remove them before they release spores.
Time fungicide applications to coincide with spore release during wet weather.
consult_expert_if: Heavy infection occurs despite timely fungicide programmes.
Fruit set is significantly reduced.

Apple___healthy.description: The leaf appears healthy with no visible signs of disease.
management: Continue regular scouting for early pest and disease detection.
Maintain balanced fertilisation and adequate irrigation.
Follow an integrated pest management (IPM) programme.
preventive_measures: Keep orchard floor clean.
Prune annually to maintain canopy structure.
Monitor for early signs of common apple diseases and pests.
consult_expert_if: Unusual symptoms appear later in the season.
Yield or fruit quality declines unexpectedly.

management: Continue regular monitoring and standard cultural practices.
preventive_measures: Maintain proper soil pH (4.5–5.5) and drainage.
consult_expert_if: Wilting, discolouration or stunting appears.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of cherry forms a white, powdery fungal coating on young leaves, shoots and sometimes fruit. Infected leaves curl or distort and may drop prematurely.
symptoms: White or grey powdery patches on leaf surfaces
Curled or distorted young leaves
Stunted shoot growth
management: Apply sulphur-based or systemic fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil) at first sign of infection.
Prune to open the canopy and improve airflow.
Avoid excess nitrogen fertilisation that promotes succulent, susceptible growth.
preventive_measures: Favour resistant varieties.
Monitor new growth closely in warm, dry weather followed by humid nights.
consult_expert_if: Infection persists despite two fungicide applications.

management: Continue regular scouting and standard IPM practices.
preventive_measures: Prune annually and maintain tree vigour.
consult_expert_if: Unexpected symptoms appear.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is a major foliar disease of maize, producing long, rectangular, tan-to-grey lesions with parallel edges, especially on lower leaves. Severe infections can cause significant yield loss.
symptoms: Rectangular, grey-tan lesions with parallel sides running between leaf veins
Lesions may coalesce in humid conditions, killing large leaf areas
Premature leaf death in severe cases
management: Plant resistant hybrids – this is the most effective management strategy.
Rotate away from maize for at least one year to reduce inoculum.
Apply foliar fungicides (e.g., strobilurin or triazole groups) at VT/R1 stage if economic threshold is reached.
Incorporate crop residue to speed decomposition of the fungal inoculum.
preventive_measures: Select hybrids with documented GLS tolerance.
Avoid continuous maize monoculture in high-humidity regions.
Scout fields from V6 onwards.
consult_expert_if: More than 50% of the leaf area on upper canopy leaves is lesioned before tasselling.
Fungicide selection or resistance management guidance is needed.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust produces small, brick-red pustules on both leaf surfaces that may rupture and release powdery spores. It is most damaging on susceptible varieties and in cool, humid climates.
symptoms: Small, oval to elongated brick-red pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture and release reddish-brown urediniospores
Heavily infected leaves turn yellow and die prematurely
management: Use resistant hybrids wherever available.
Apply foliar fungicides (triazoles, strobilurins) if disease is severe and crop is at a susceptible stage.
Early planting can help the crop escape peak rust pressure.
preventive_measures: Monitor fields from V6 stage, particularly in cooler weather.
Scout particularly after wet periods with moderate temperatures (16–23 °C).
consult_expert_if: Pustules appear before tasselling on a susceptible hybrid.
Disease spreads to the ear leaves rapidly.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight causes large, cigar-shaped, tan-grey lesions on maize leaves. Severe infections before or during grain fill can substantially reduce yield.
symptoms: Long (2.5–15 cm), tan to grey, cigar-shaped lesions
Dark green, water-soaked borders initially
Green-black fungal sporulation within lesions in humid weather
management: Plant NLB-resistant hybrids.
Rotate crops to reduce residue-borne inoculum.
Apply foliar fungicides (triazole or strobilurin) at first sign of disease on susceptible hybrids.
Manage crop residue by tillage or incorporation.
preventive_measures: Scout from V8 stage.
Avoid irrigating in late afternoon – wet foliage overnight promotes infection.
consult_expert_if: Upper canopy leaves are heavily infected before mid-grain fill.
Fungicide resistance is suspected.

management: Continue regular scouting and follow IPM guidelines.
preventive_measures: Rotate crops and use certified seed.
consult_expert_if: Unexplained wilting, stalk softening or discolouration appears.

Grape___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a destructive fungal disease of grapes that causes leaf spots, shoot lesions, and fruit rot. Infected berries shrivel into hard, black mummies.
symptoms: Tan to brown circular leaf spots with dark borders
Black, shrivelled mummified berries
Dark lesions on shoots and petioles
management: Remove and destroy mummified fruit from the vine and ground before budbreak.
Apply protectant or systemic fungicides (e.g., myclobutanil, mancozeb) from budbreak through berry set.
Prune vines to improve canopy airflow.
Eliminate sources of primary inoculum by removing infected wood.
preventive_measures: Maintain good vineyard sanitation.
Train vines to promote quick drying of foliage.
Apply a dormant spray if mummies cannot be fully removed.
consult_expert_if: More than 5% of berries are mummified at harvest.
Disease persists despite a full spray programme.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).pathogen: Fungal complex: Phaeomoniella chlamydospora, Phaeoacremonium spp., Fomitiporia mediterranea
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a trunk disease complex causing chronic foliar symptoms (tiger-stripe discolouration), berries with dark spots, and internal wood decay. It can lead to vine death.
symptoms: Interveinal leaf discolouration with yellow/red margins (tiger-stripe pattern)
Dark, sunken spots on ripe berries (measles symptom)
Sudden wilting and death of individual arms or whole vines (apoplexy)
Brown streaking in cross-sections of infected wood
management: There is currently no curative treatment for established Esca infections.
Remove and destroy severely affected vines to limit spread.
Prune during dry weather and seal large pruning wounds with commercial wound protectants.
Consider double-pruning strategies to delay wood exposure during moist conditions.
preventive_measures: Use clean, certified propagation material.
Protect pruning wounds immediately after cutting.
Avoid pruning during rainy or humid weather.
consult_expert_if: Apoplexy (sudden vine collapse) occurs.
More than 10% of vines show symptoms.
Replanting decisions need to be made.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight causes angular to irregular brown or tan spots on leaves, which may lead to premature defoliation and reduced photosynthetic capacity.
symptoms: Angular, dark brown spots on older leaves
Yellowing around lesions
Premature leaf drop in severe cases
management: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Apply copper-based or approved fungicides as a protectant measure.
Improve canopy airflow through timely shoot positioning and leaf removal.
preventive_measures: Maintain canopy management to reduce humidity.
Avoid excessive irrigation.
consult_expert_if: Rapid defoliation threatens fruit ripening.
Disease identity needs laboratory confirmation.

management: Continue monitoring and standard IPM programme.
preventive_measures: Maintain canopy management and vineyard sanitation.
consult_expert_if: Unusual symptoms appear.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).pathogen: Bacterium: Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (vector: Asian citrus psyllid)
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB), also known as citrus greening, is a devastating bacterial disease spread by the Asian citrus psyllid. There is currently no cure; infected trees decline progressively.
symptoms: Asymmetric (blotchy) yellowing of leaves (not uniform chlorosis)
Stunted, upright shoots (flush) with small, yellowed leaves
Lopsided, bitter, green-coloured fruit that stays green even at maturity
Progressive tree decline and death within 5–8 years
management: Remove and destroy infected trees promptly to prevent spread.
Control the Asian citrus psyllid vector using insecticides and/or biological control.
Apply nutritional programmes (foliar micronutrients) to prolong productivity of mildly affected trees.
Use only certified, disease-free nursery stock for replanting.
preventive_measures: Install psyllid monitoring traps in the grove.
Source trees exclusively from certified, screenhouse-grown nurseries.
Enforce quarantine regulations on movement of citrus plant material.
consult_expert_if: Suspicious blotchy mottling is observed.
Psyllid populations are detected.
Tree removal and replanting decisions are needed.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot causes water-soaked spots on peach leaves that turn dark and fall out, leaving a shot-hole appearance. Fruit develop dark, sunken lesions that reduce marketability.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked leaf spots that turn dark brown with a yellow halo
Shot-hole appearance as lesion centres fall out
Dark, sunken lesions on fruit surface
Cankers on twigs in severe infections
management: Apply copper-based bactericides during the growing season (consult local extension for timing).
Select resistant or tolerant varieties for new plantings.
Prune out infected shoots during dry weather and destroy prunings.
Avoid excessive nitrogen – overly vigorous growth is more susceptible.
preventive_measures: Avoid overhead irrigation.
Apply preventive copper sprays before wet weather periods.
Maintain moderate tree vigour through balanced fertilisation.
consult_expert_if: Twig cankers appear and spread rapidly.
Significant fruit crop loss occurs despite a spray programme.
Variety selection advice is needed for replanting.

management: Continue monitoring and follow standard orchard IPM practices.
preventive_measures: Prune annually and monitor for early disease or pest signs.
consult_expert_if: Unexpected symptoms appear.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.pathogen: Bacterium: Xanthomonas euvesicatoria (and related Xanthomonas spp.)
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of pepper causes water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit that turn brown with a yellow halo. Severe infections cause early defoliation and fruit surface blemishes.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked lesions on leaves and fruit
Lesions turn brown to black with yellow halos
Raised, rough scab-like spots on fruit
Premature defoliation in severe infections
management: Use disease-free transplants from certified sources.
Apply copper-based bactericides on a preventive schedule.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least two years.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
preventive_measures: Treat seeds with hot water (52 °C for 30 minutes) before planting.
Avoid working in the field when foliage is wet.
Remove and destroy infected plant debris at season end.
consult_expert_if: Copper-resistant strains are suspected (disease continues despite copper sprays).
Widespread defoliation threatens yield.

management: Maintain monitoring and standard cultural practices.
preventive_measures: Rotate crops and use certified transplants.
consult_expert_if: Wilting, spots or abnormal growth appears.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common foliar disease of potato characterised by dark, concentric-ringed lesions on older leaves. It typically appears after tuber initiation under hot, dry weather interspersed with rain.
symptoms: Dark brown to black lesions with concentric rings (target-board pattern) on older leaves
Yellow halo surrounding lesions
Lesions start on lower leaves and progress upward
Severe defoliation reduces tuber yield and quality
management: Apply preventive fungicides (e.g., chlorothalonil, mancozeb) once disease risk is high.
Maintain adequate plant nutrition – well-nourished plants are more tolerant.
Remove infected plant debris promptly.
Use certified disease-free seed tubers.
preventive_measures: Plant certified seed and rotate crops annually.
Avoid water stress during the growing season.
Scout plants regularly from mid-season.
consult_expert_if: Defoliation exceeds 30% before canopy closure.
Fungicide efficacy appears reduced.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a devastating oomycete disease historically responsible for the Irish Famine. It spreads explosively in cool, wet conditions, destroying foliage and tubers within days if untreated.
symptoms: Pale green to dark brown water-soaked lesions on leaves, often at margins
White to grey sporulation on the underside of lesions in humid conditions
Rapid browning and collapse of foliage
Brown, greasy internal rot of tubers
management: Apply systemic fungicides (e.g., metalaxyl-M, dimethomorph) at first sign of infection – timing is critical.
Alternate with protectant fungicides to manage resistance.
Destroy infected foliage before harvest to protect tubers.
Use resistant varieties (check local extension recommendations).
preventive_measures: Monitor late blight forecasting systems and apply preventive sprays before infection periods.
Plant certified disease-free seed tubers.
Avoid overhead irrigation in the afternoon.
Ensure good field drainage.
consult_expert_if: Lesions appear during a forecasted infection period without prior fungicide coverage.
More than 10% of plants show symptoms.
Tuber infection is detected at harvest.

management: Continue scouting and standard cultural practices.
preventive_measures: Rotate crops and use certified seed.
consult_expert_if: Wilting, dark spots or tuber symptoms appear.

management: Maintain monitoring and follow standard cane management practices.
preventive_measures: Prune old canes and maintain good airflow.
consult_expert_if: Unusual spots or cane dieback appears.

management: Continue monitoring and follow standard soybean IPM guidelines.
preventive_measures: Rotate with non-legume crops and use certified seed.
consult_expert_if: Yellowing, wilting or pod symptoms appear.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.pathogen: Fungi: Podosphaera xanthii and Erysiphe cichoracearum
Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Powdery mildew of squash and cucurbits appears as white, powdery fungal growth on leaf surfaces. It spreads rapidly in warm, dry conditions with high relative humidity at night.
symptoms: White, powdery fungal patches on upper leaf surfaces
Yellowing and browning of leaves as infection progresses
Premature leaf senescence and reduced fruit quality
management: Apply sulphur or potassium bicarbonate fungicides at first sign.
Systemic fungicides (e.g., triazoles) can be used if infection is severe.
Remove heavily infected leaves.
Plant resistant varieties.
preventive_measures: Avoid planting in low-airflow areas.
Water in the morning to allow foliage to dry during the day.
Monitor from mid-season onwards.
consult_expert_if: Plants collapse before fruit maturity.
Multiple fungicide applications fail to control the disease.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Leaf scorch produces small, irregular, dark purple spots on strawberry leaves that coalesce, giving a scorched appearance. Severe infections weaken plants and reduce berry yield.
symptoms: Small, irregular dark purple to red spots on leaves
Spots enlarge and centres turn tan or grey
Confluent lesions give a scorched appearance
Premature defoliation in severe cases
management: Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Apply fungicides (e.g., captan or pyraclostrobin) on a protective schedule.
Renovate matted-row planting after harvest.
Plant resistant varieties.
preventive_measures: Avoid overhead irrigation.
Improve row spacing and airflow.
Mulch around plants to reduce soil-splash inoculum.
consult_expert_if: Widespread leaf death occurs before harvest.
Crowns appear water-soaked or rotted (may indicate a different disease).

management: Continue standard strawberry management practices.
preventive_measures: Renovate planting after harvest; replace old crowns.
consult_expert_if: Spots, wilting or root problems appear.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.pathogen: Bacterium: Xanthomonas vesicatoria and related species
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is a common tomato disease causing dark, water-soaked leaf and fruit lesions. It spreads by rain splash and physical contact.
symptoms: Small, dark, water-soaked spots on leaves with yellow halos
Spots turn brown, dry and may crack
Raised, scabby lesions on green fruit
Defoliation and reduced fruit set in severe infections
management: Apply copper-based bactericides preventively.
Avoid overhead irrigation and working in wet fields.
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops.
Use disease-free transplants.
preventive_measures: Hot-water seed treatment (52 °C for 30 minutes).
Stake and prune plants for good airflow.
Apply mulch to reduce soil-splash.
consult_expert_if: Copper resistance is confirmed by laboratory testing.
More than 30% of plants are defoliated.

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a very common tomato disease, characterised by dark concentric-ringed lesions (bulls-eye pattern) on older leaves. It progresses upwards and can cause significant defoliation.
symptoms: Dark, circular lesions with concentric rings on older leaves
Yellow halo around lesions
Stem and fruit can also be infected
Premature leaf drop from the base upwards
management: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin) on a 7–10-day schedule.
Remove infected lower leaves and dispose of them away from the field.
Maintain adequate nutrition, especially nitrogen.
Stake plants to keep foliage off the soil.
preventive_measures: Use certified disease-free transplants.
Rotate away from Solanaceae for 2–3 years.
Mulch the soil surface to reduce splash inoculum.
Avoid overhead irrigation.
consult_expert_if: Disease progresses rapidly despite fungicide treatment.
Upper canopy leaves are affected before fruit set.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a destructive disease of tomatoes, capable of destroying entire fields within a week under cool, wet conditions. It is the same pathogen that caused the Irish Famine.
symptoms: Irregular, greasy-looking, dark-green to brown lesions on leaves
White sporulation on underside of lesions in humid conditions
Brown, firm lesions on tomato fruit
Rapid collapse of foliage in favourable conditions
management: Apply systemic fungicides (metalaxyl-M, dimethomorph, fluopicolide) immediately at first detection.
Alternate fungicide groups to manage resistance.
Destroy severely infected plants promptly.
Do not plant tomatoes in field areas with confirmed infection until rotation is complete.
preventive_measures: Monitor weather-based late blight forecasting services.
Apply protective fungicides before expected infection periods.
Ensure good plant spacing and staking for airflow.
Remove and destroy volunteer potato or tomato plants.
consult_expert_if: Infection spreads despite fungicide coverage.
Metalaxyl resistance is suspected.
Entire field shows symptoms.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Leaf mold is a greenhouse and tunnel tomato disease favoured by high humidity. It produces distinctive yellow patches on upper leaf surfaces with olive-green to grey-brown velvety sporulation on the undersides.
symptoms: Pale yellow-green patches on upper leaf surfaces
Olive-green to grey-brown velvety sporulation on leaf undersides
Infected leaves yellow and wither
Rarely affects fruit, but can cause blossom drop
management: Reduce humidity through ventilation and heating (in protected crops).
Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or difenoconazole) if ventilation alone is insufficient.
Remove and destroy infected leaves.
Space plants adequately and train side-shoots to improve airflow.
preventive_measures: Plant resistant varieties (races differ – confirm race present locally).
Avoid overhead irrigation in tunnels.
Disinfect structures and equipment between cropping seasons.
consult_expert_if: More than 25% of leaf area is affected.
Disease appears resistant to standard fungicides.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot causes numerous small, circular spots with dark borders and light-grey centres on tomato leaves. It spreads upward from lower leaves and can cause severe defoliation.
symptoms: Small, circular spots (3–5 mm) with dark borders and grey-white centres
Tiny black pycnidia (spore bodies) visible in lesion centres
Yellowing and browning of heavily infected leaves
Progressive defoliation from the base upward
management: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, copper-based) on a regular schedule.
Remove infected lower leaves.
Stake plants and manage canopy for airflow.
Mulch soil surface to reduce splash.
preventive_measures: Rotate away from Solanaceae for 2 years.
Use certified disease-free transplants.
Avoid working in the field when plants are wet.
consult_expert_if: Defoliation reaches the upper canopy before fruit maturity.
Disease does not respond to standard fungicide programme.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Two-spotted spider mites are tiny arachnids that cause stippling, bronzing and eventual necrosis of tomato leaves. They thrive in hot, dry conditions and can rapidly colonise plants.
symptoms: Fine, pale yellow stippling on upper leaf surfaces
Bronze to brown leaf discolouration in heavy infestations
Fine silk webbing on leaf undersides and between leaves
Tiny moving dots (mites) visible on leaf undersides
management: Apply miticides (abamectin, bifenazate, spiromesifen) on a rotation to manage resistance.
Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiidae) as biological control in protected crops.
Ensure adequate irrigation – water-stressed plants are more susceptible.
Avoid pesticides that kill natural mite predators.
preventive_measures: Scout leaf undersides from mid-season.
Maintain adequate soil moisture.
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt natural enemies.
consult_expert_if: Miticide applications fail to control the population.
Resistance management recommendations are needed.

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot causes brown, target-like lesions on leaves, stems and fruit of tomatoes. It is favoured by warm, humid conditions and can cause significant defoliation.
symptoms: Brown circular to irregular lesions with concentric rings on leaves
Dark brown lesions on stems and petioles
Sunken, brown fruit lesions
Premature defoliation
management: Apply fungicides (azoxystrobin, chlorothalonil, or fluxapyroxad) on a preventive schedule.
Remove and dispose of infected plant material.
Improve canopy ventilation.
preventive_measures: Use certified transplants.
Rotate away from Solanaceae.
Avoid prolonged leaf wetness.
consult_expert_if: Significant defoliation occurs before fruit maturity.
Fungicide rotation advice is needed.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.pathogen: Virus: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (vector: Bemisia tabaci – silverleaf whitefly)
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: TYLCV is a destructive geminivirus spread by silverleaf whiteflies. Infected plants are severely stunted with upward-curled, yellowed leaves and dramatically reduced fruit set. There is no cure.
symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of young leaves
Severely stunted plant growth
Flower drop and very few fruit
Small, pale green leaves on new growth
management: Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to reduce inoculum source.
Control whitefly vector with systemic insecticides (imidacloprid, thiamethoxam) or insect-growth regulators.
Use reflective silver mulch to deter whiteflies.
Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties.
preventive_measures: Use resistant or tolerant varieties.
Install yellow sticky traps to monitor whitefly levels.
Establish whitefly-free transplants from screened nurseries.
Remove crop debris promptly after harvest.
consult_expert_if: More than 10% of plants are infected early in the season.
Whitefly populations are not controlled by insecticides (resistance suspected).
Variety selection for your local TYLCV strain is needed.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: ToMV is a mechanically transmitted tobamovirus causing mosaic discolouration, leaf distortion and reduced fruit quality in tomatoes. It is highly stable in soil and plant debris.
symptoms: Mosaic pattern of light and dark green on leaves
Leaf distortion, fern-like narrowing or blistering
Stunted plant growth
Internal browning of fruit in some strains
management: There is no curative treatment; remove and destroy infected plants.
Wash hands, tools and clothing thoroughly before entering the field or greenhouse.
Use virus-indexed seed and certified transplants.
Plant ToMV-resistant varieties (R genes Tm-1, Tm-2, Tm-2²).
preventive_measures: Avoid using tobacco products near tomatoes – tobacco carries related viruses.
Disinfect tools with bleach solution (10%) or milk between plants.
Control aphid and thrips vectors.
Remove and destroy all crop residues after harvest.
consult_expert_if: Rapid spread through the planting is observed.
Virus identity needs laboratory confirmation.
Replacement variety options are needed.

management: Continue regular scouting and standard IPM practices.
preventive_measures: Rotate crops annually.
Use certified transplants.
Monitor for early signs of disease and pests.
consult_expert_if: Any unusual symptoms appear on leaves, stems or fruit.
